bib.title: Contextual Bandits (Chapter 18, Bandit Algorithms)
bib.venue: Bandit Algorithms, Cambridge University Press (book chapter)

question: How should regret be defined and minimised in k-armed bandits when a context is observed each round, so the learner competes with context-dependent policies?
contributions: Contextual regret as best context-dependent policy in hindsight (Eq 18.1, 18.5)
Exp4 algorithm and regret bound sqrt(2nk log M)
Data-dependent bound via expert agreement E*_n (Theorem 18.3)

results.claim: Exp4 with gamma=0 and eta=sqrt(2 log(M)/(nk)) has expected regret at most sqrt(2nk log M) against the best of M oblivious experts.
results.setup: k-armed adversarial bandit, rewards in [0,1], M oblivious experts, known horizon n, gamma=0
results.note: Quote is the theorem's first line; the bound itself is split across lines in the text. Book proof, so kind measured is used for the book's own derivation.

results.claim: Per-context Exp3 gives regret at most 2 sqrt(nk|C| log k) when all contexts are equally frequent, and the bound is vacuous for n <= 4k|C| log(k).
results.setup: Finite context set C, one anytime Exp3 per context, adversarial rewards in [0,1]^k

results.claim: Applying Exp4 to all functions C->[k] (M = k^|C|) recovers the sqrt(2nk|C| log k) bound; for any finite policy class Phi the regret is at most sqrt(2nk log|Phi|), with C possibly infinite.
results.quote: if C is arbitrary (possibly inﬁnite) and Φ is a ﬁnite set

results.claim: With time-varying learning rate eta_t = sqrt(log(M)/E*_t), Exp4 has data-dependent regret at most C sqrt(E*_n log M), where E*_n <= n min(k,M) measures expert disagreement; the algorithm is anytime.
results.setup: Same as Thm 18.1; E*_t = sum_s sum_i max_m E_mi; C a universal constant; proof left as Exercise 18.4

results.claim: In the stochastic (iid context/reward) contextual bandit with an ERM optimisation oracle, explore-then-commit gets O(n^{2/3}) regret; Agarwal et al. 2014 achieve about the sqrt(nk log|Phi|) rate in polynomial time.
results.source: Agarwal et al. 2014; Langford and Zhang 2008 (epoch-greedy)
results.setup: iid context/reward pairs, finite policy class Phi, argmax oracle; Exercise 18.8 gives O(n^2/3 (k log|Phi|)^1/3)

limits: Chapter focuses on the k-armed adversarial model; stochastic contextual bandits only in Notes 5 and Exercises 18.8-18.9.
No linear contextual bandit or LinUCB treatment in this chapter (linear/stochastic linear bandits come in later chapters).
Exp4 uses O(M) memory and O(M+k) time per round, impractical for large M or k.
Experts assumed oblivious; non-oblivious case only via weaker regret R'_n (Exercise 18.6).
High-probability bounds and lower bounds not developed (Note 8); no experiments.
practices: Choose the competitor class Phi to trade meaningfulness of regret against learning cost; larger class means larger regret (Notes 1).
With finite contexts and enough data, run one anytime Exp3 per context; ignore context when n is small (18.1).
With large structured context sets, define a policy/expert class (partitions, similarity functions, or supervised-learned predictors) and run Exp4 over it (18.2).
Use Exp4 as a building block by defining your own experts (Note 2).
For stochastic contexts, reduce to cost-sensitive ERM using an optimisation oracle (Note 5).

terms.definition: Regret against the best context-dependent policy in hindsight, R_n = E[sum_c max_i sum_{t:c_t=c}(x_ti - X_t)] (Eq 18.1)
k-armed adversarial bandit where M experts announce distributions over actions each round; regret against the best expert (Eq 18.6); contextual bandits arise when experts are static C->[k] maps
Exponential weighting for exploration and exploitation with experts: keep distribution Q_t over experts, play P_t = Q_t E(t), update Q by exponential weighting of propagated reward estimates
Exp4 with gamma>0 (implicit exploration), left to Exercise 18.3 for high-probability bounds
Sum over rounds and actions of the max over experts of their probability on that action; effective-number-of-experts measure, E*_n <= n min(k,M)

lineage.note: Exp4 introduced there; Theorem 18.1 matches their theorem 7.1 with a slightly smaller constant
